# Seaweed

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="seaweed-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="seaweed-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="seaweed-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Inorganic arsenic is the metal to check in seaweed: hijiki carries about 47–77 mg/kg as sold, while nori, wakame and most kombu measure about 0.1–0.3 mg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Survey of Inorganic Arsenic in Seaweed and Seaweed-Containing Products Available in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ), Survey report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Inorganic arsenic in hijiki and oarweed; cadmium in laver and wakame; lead and mercury usually low.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Seaweed type and kelp species, growing water and tissue age, and preparation.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaughnessy B K, Jackson B P, Byrnes J E K · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals">Evidence of elevated heavy metals concentrations in wild and farmed sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) in New England</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Avoid hijiki, name the kelp species, and ask for inorganic arsenic and cadmium results.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
</ul>
</section>


<a id="decision-summary"></a>
## Seaweed overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Inorganic arsenic decides most seaweed questions, and it depends far more on the type of seaweed than on where it was bought. Hijiki is the clear outlier: nine retail hijiki products in the United Kingdom averaged 77 mg/kg inorganic arsenic as sold, and WHO GEMS/Food hijiki submissions had a median of 47 mg/kg (10 results, 2010–2024).<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Nori, wakame and most kombu sold in Australia and Europe measured about 0.1–0.3 mg/kg, two to three orders of magnitude lower on the same dried-as-sold basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Survey of Inorganic Arsenic in Seaweed and Seaweed-Containing Products Available in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ), Survey report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Total arsenic is high in almost every seaweed but is mostly organic arsenosugars, so a total arsenic result cannot stand in for inorganic arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/garcia-salgado2012-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">García-Salgado S, Quijano MA, Bonilla MM · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/garcia-salgado2012-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation">Arsenic speciation in edible alga samples by microwave-assisted extraction and high performance liquid chromatography coupled to atomic fluorescence spectrometry</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Analytica Chimica Acta</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/garcia-salgado2012-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/taylor2016-new-england-seaweed-arsenic|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Taylor VF, Jackson BP · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/taylor2016-new-england-seaweed-arsenic">Concentrations and speciation of arsenic in New England seaweed species harvested for food and agriculture</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemosphere</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/taylor2016-new-england-seaweed-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Dried kombu in GEMS/Food had a median of 47 mg/kg total arsenic while the same dried-kombu category had a median of 0.23 mg/kg inorganic arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Two kelps break the pattern: Norwegian oarweed (Laminaria digitata) had a median of 21 mg/kg inorganic arsenic dry weight, against 0.037 mg/kg in tangle (Laminaria hyperborea) from the same monitoring programme.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cadmium is the second metal to watch and it ranks the types differently. In European monitoring, dried laver (nori) averaged 1.68 mg/kg cadmium and dried wakame 1.28 mg/kg, against 0.46 mg/kg in dried kombu, so the lowest inorganic arsenic types are not the lowest cadmium types.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Lead and mercury are usually low: most dried-seaweed mercury results in GEMS/Food were below a 50 µg/kg detection limit, and dried nori lead had a median of about 0.14 mg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For buyers, the supported priorities are to avoid hijiki or require an inorganic arsenic result for it, to specify the kelp species, and to ask for a cadmium result on nori, wakame and laver products.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, ## Seaweed identity and scope

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers edible marine macroalgae: brown seaweeds such as kombu and other kelps (Laminaria, Saccharina), wakame (Undaria), hijiki (Sargassum fusiforme), arame and the wracks (Fucus, Ascophyllum); red seaweeds such as nori and laver (Porphyra, Pyropia), dulse and Irish moss; and green seaweeds such as sea lettuce (Ulva).<sup The basis matters as much as the type. Fresh seaweed is roughly 85% water, so a fresh-weight concentration is several times lower than a dry-weight one for the same plant, and Australia and New Zealand express their seaweed limit at 85% hydration.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Survey of Inorganic Arsenic in Seaweed and Seaweed-Containing Products Available in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ), Survey report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2024-schedule-19-contaminants|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2024-schedule-19-contaminants">Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code - <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-seaweed" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-seaweed-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one seaweed group and metal; a mean, median and range from the same samples are separate rows. Total and inorganic arsenic are separate metals. Dry-weight, dried-as-sold and wet results are never mixed. Ratings place a reported mean, median or sample result against a pooled HMI reference for the same metal and basis, built from every compatible seaweed sampling family. Same-study contrasts compare a subgroup with its own study total. Held rows failed a check against their own paper and are shown but not compared.</p>

data-shared-occurrence-methods><summary>Shared dataset methods and interpretation</summary><div data-shared-evidence-content><p>Source summaries retain their original statistic, material, basis and censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:seaweed-iAs-dried-product-as-sold:3cd5a62169c9"><summary>HMI seaweed iAs reference (dried product as sold) · 5 sampling families</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:seaweed-iAs-dried-product-as-sold:3cd5a62169c9"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI seaweed iAs reference (dried product as sold) · 5 sampling families. Dried product as sold, µg/kg; no basis conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤50</td><td>100–200 (bounded)</td><td>2400</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤50</td><td>90–290 (bounded)</td><td>2400</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>142 reference units; 5 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>81</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>FSANZ 2010 seaweed survey</td><td>18</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>McSheehy et al. 2000</td><td>10</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Rose et al. 2007</td><td>31</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Matsumoto-Tanibuchi et al. 2019</td><td>2</td><td>20%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians from every compatible seaweed sampling family in the evidence ledger on one basis (dried product as sold): WHO GEMS/Food medians by seaweed type, product form, WHO region and year (random sampling only), individual sample results printed by surveys, and published subgroup medians. All edible macroalgal types are pooled, so a position shows where a result sits among seaweeds in general; types differ systematically. Each family has equal total weight; subgroups have equal weight within a family. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>An international evidence-library reference across seaweed types, not a probability sample of any market. Hijiki and some kelps dominate the upper arsenic tail. GEMS/Food regions are reporting regions, not growing origins. Different bases are never mixed. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li><li><a href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au" class="internal" data-slug="sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au" data-no-cite-meta>FSANZ 2010 seaweed survey</a></li><li><a href="../sources/mcsheehy2000-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation" class="internal" data-slug="sources/mcsheehy2000-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation" data-no-cite-meta>McSheehy et al. 2000</a></li><li><a href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk" class="internal" data-slug="sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk" data-no-cite-meta>Rose et al. 2007</a></li><li><a href="../sources/matsumoto-tanibuchi2019-seaweed-seafood-ias" class="internal" data-slug="sources/matsumoto-tanibuchi2019-seaweed-seafood-ias" data-no-cite-meta>Matsumoto-Tanibuchi et al. 2019</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>hmi-pooled-reference-v2:seaweed-iAs-dried-product-as-sold:3cd5a62169c9</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. It describes the evidence currently in this scope; it is not a worldwide or current-lot benchmark. Source, year and region filters do not change it. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:seaweed-iAs-dry-weight:4e2abe137da9"><summary>HMI seaweed iAs reference (dry weight) · 10 sampling families</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:seaweed-iAs-dry-weight:4e2abe137da9"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI seaweed iAs reference (dry weight) · 10 sampling families. <a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>

→</a></span></span></sup> In Norwegian monitoring, wireweed (Sargassum muticum) had a median of 51 mg/kg inorganic arsenic dry weight and imported hijiki 59 mg/kg, while the other species had medians of 0.23 mg/kg or less except oarweed and sea oak (7.6 mg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Inorganic arsenic in farmed Chinese hijiki rose through the season, from 40 mg/kg in January to 58 mg/kg dry weight in May.<sup class="cite">[[sources/huang2020-hijiki-arsenic-growth-stages|22]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Huang SX, Jiang Q, Ding YF, Wang FJ, Zhu C · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/huang2020-hijiki-arsenic-growth-stages">Arsenic contents and speciation at different growth stages of Sargassum fusiforme [Harv.] Setchell (Hijiki), an edible seaweed</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Ecology and Environmental Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/huang2020-hijiki-arsenic-growth-stages">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cadmium and lead follow local water and tissue age. In New England sugar kelp, the young base of the blade carried more cadmium and total arsenic than the old tip at every site, while lead and mercury were higher at known contaminated sites.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaughnessy B K, Jackson B P, Byrnes J E K · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals">Evidence of elevated heavy metals concentrations in wild and farmed sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) in New England</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In the Salish Sea, lead exceeded 9 mg/kg dry weight only at shipyard and harbour sites, and bull kelp at the same sites carried about twice the cadmium of rockweed.<sup class="cite">[[sources/hahn2022-salish-seaweed-contaminants|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Hahn ME, Schultz IR, Ylitalo GM, Boyd D, Sloan CA, Niewolny LA, Bolton JL, Haigh T, Incardona JP · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/hahn2022-salish-seaweed-contaminants">Chemical contaminant levels in edible seaweeds of the Salish Sea and implications for their consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLOS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/hahn2022-salish-seaweed-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Within kelp, species matters more than origin. Oarweed (Laminaria digitata) had 21 mg/kg inorganic arsenic dry weight in Norway, 30–62 mg/kg in Irish blades and 8.3 mg/kg in Maine, while tangle, sugar kelp and Japanese kombu (Saccharina) were at 0.02–0.16 mg/kg in Norway.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe Cadmium reverses part of that order. Dried laver had the highest cadmium mean among European seaweed groups (1.68 mg/kg) and dried wakame was next (1.28 mg/kg), while dried kombu averaged 0.46 mg/kg and dulse 0.46 mg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In a Canary Islands market survey, kombu and wakame of declared Galician origin averaged 0.085 and 0.070 mg/kg cadmium dry weight against 0.42 and 0.75 mg/kg for Asian kombu and wakame, about five and eleven times lower, a within-study origin difference that has not been tested elsewhere.<sup class="cite">[[sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Martín-León V, Paz S, D&#39;Eufemia PA, Plasencia JJ, Sagratini G, Marcantoni G, Navarro-Romero M, Gutiérrez ÁJ, Hardisson A, Rubio-Armendáriz C · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates">Human Exposure to Toxic Metals (Cd, Pb, Hg) and Nitrates (NO3−) from Seaweed Consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are tentative origin patterns from one study, not a reliable sourcing preference for a country.

class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-seaweeds-have-the-lowest-inorganic-arsenic" data-anchor="which-seaweeds-have-the-lowest-inorganic-arsenic" data-question="Which seaweeds have the lowest inorganic arsenic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which seaweeds have the lowest inorganic arsenic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Nori, wakame, dulse and Saccharina kombu were lowest, at about 0.1–0.3 mg/kg in Australian and European dried products as sold and 0.02–0.16 mg/kg dry weight in Norwegian monitoring.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Survey of Inorganic Arsenic in Seaweed and Seaweed-Containing Products Available in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ), Survey report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fsanz2012-seaweed-inorganic-arsenic-au">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gomez Ruiz JA · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2023-heavy-metals-seaweed">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Rockweed (Ascophyllum) was also low, mostly below 0.07 mg/kg dry weight in Irish samples.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ronan JM, Stengel DB, Raab A, Feldmann J, O&#39;Hea L, Bralatei E, McGovern E · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland">High proportions of inorganic arsenic in Laminaria digitata href="../sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> These are the lowest observed types in each study; a single product can still differ, so a result for the lot is the reliable check.

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="is-all-kelp-high-in-arsenic" data-anchor="is-all-kelp-high-in-arsenic" data-question="Is all kelp high in arsenic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Is all kelp high in arsenic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

No. All kelps carry tens of mg/kg total arsenic, but inorganic arsenic ranges from about 0.02 mg/kg in Norwegian Saccharina kombu to 21 mg/kg in oarweed, and up to 87 mg/kg in decaying Irish oarweed tips.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ronan JM, Stengel DB, Raab A, Feldmann J, O&#39;Hea L, Bralatei E, McGovern E · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland">High proportions of inorganic arsenic in Laminaria digitata but not in Ascophyllum nodosum samples from Ireland</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemosphere</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ronan2017-laminaria-ascophyllum-ias-ireland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The species name, not the word kelp, decides the inorganic arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-origin-change-cadmium-in-nori-and-wakame" data-anchor="does-origin-change-cadmium-in-nori-and-wakame" data-question="Does origin change cadmium in nori and wakame?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does origin change cadmium in nori and wakame?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Possibly. In one Canary Islands survey, Asian kombu and wakame had about five and eleven times the cadmium of Galician products, and Korean laver from the west coast averaged 0.69 mg/kg against 0.50 mg/kg from the south coast.<sup class="cite">[[sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Martín-León V, Paz S, D&#39;Eufemia PA, Plasencia JJ, Sagratini G, Marcantoni G, Navarro-Romero M, Gutiérrez ÁJ, Hardisson A, Rubio-Armendáriz C · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates">Human Exposure to Toxic Metals (Cd, Pb, Hg) and Nitrates (NO3−) from Seaweed Consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martinleon2021-edible-seaweeds-canary-metals-nitrates">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/hwang2010-dried-seaweed-korea-metals|26]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Hwang YO, Park SG, Park GY, Choi SM, Kim MY · 2010</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/hwang2010-dried-seaweed-korea-metals">Total arsenic, mercury, lead, and cadmium contents in edible dried seaweed in Korea</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Additives &amp; Contaminants: Part B: Surveillance</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/hwang2010-dried-seaweed-korea-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Neither difference has been confirmed by another study.

</div>
</details>



<a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Processing effects and seaweed derivatives

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Soaking and boiling move arsenic out of seaweed into the water, and the water is where it ends up.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Laparra JM, Velez D, Montoro R, Barbera R, Farre R · 2003</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Estimation of Arsenic Bioaccessibility in Edible Seaweed by an in Vitro Digestion Method</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ownsworth E, Selby D, Ottley CJ, Unsworth E, Raab A, Feldmann J, Sproson AD, Kuroda J, Faidutti C, Bucker P · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Tracing the natural and anthropogenic influence on the trace elemental chemistry of estuarine macroalgae and the implications for human consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Japanese-style soaking of dried hijiki eluted 22–32% of total arsenic, and boiling the soaked hijiki eluted a further 53–62%, mostly as arsenate.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Boiling dried hijiki for 20 minutes lowered inorganic arsenic from 54 to 31 mg/kg dry weight, while baking nori did not change its arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Laparra JM, Velez D, Montoro R, Barbera R, Farre R · 2003</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Estimation of Arsenic Bioaccessibility in Edible Seaweed by an in Vitro Digestion Method</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Commercial processing of hijiki makes a large difference. Open-steamed Japanese hijiki products carried 9–14 mg/kg water-soluble inorganic arsenic dry weight against 51–71 mg/kg for boiled or closed-steam products.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shimoda2010-commercial-hijiki-arsenic-speciation|25]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shimoda Y, Suzuki Y, Endo Y, Kato K, Tachikawa M, Endo G, Yamanaka K · 2010</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shimoda2010-commercial-hijiki-arsenic-speciation">Speciation Analysis of Arsenics in Commercial Hijiki by High Performance Liquid Chromatography-tandem-mass Spectrometry and High Performance Liquid Chromatography-inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Health Science 56(1):47-56</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shimoda2010-commercial-hijiki-arsenic-speciation">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Scottish and Japanese kelp, a soup preparation removed 75–96% of inorganic arsenic from the solid seaweed, a 10–20 second blanch 3–61% and a cold soak about 65%.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ownsworth E, Selby D, Ottley CJ, Unsworth E, Raab A, Feldmann J, Sproson AD, Kuroda J, Faidutti C, Bucker P · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Tracing the natural and anthropogenic influence on the trace elemental chemistry of estuarine macroalgae and the implications for human consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cadmium and lead respond much less. Pulsed electric field and warm-water treatment of Norwegian sugar kelp lowered iodine by up to 25% but did not lower cadmium, mercury or lead on a dry-weight basis; cadmium rose from 0.33 to 0.43 mg/kg after warm water.<sup class="cite">[[sources/sund2026-saccharina-pte-processing|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Sund R, Holdt S L, Bang-Berthelsen C H, Stevant P, Sloth J J, Skipnes D · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/sund2026-saccharina-pte-processing">Pulsed electric field processing as an alternative to warm water treatment for the reduction of potentially toxic elements in Saccharina latissima</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Applied Phycology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/sund2026-saccharina-pte-processing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Boiling Alaria in Nunavik lowered total arsenic but not cadmium, lead or mercury, and the arsenic moved into the broth.<sup class="cite">[[sources/groleau2025-inuit-fish-broth-metals-pregnancy|27]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Groleau T, Lemire M, Ponton DE, Amyot M · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/groleau2025-inuit-fish-broth-metals-pregnancy">Improving nutritional intakes and reducing metal(loid) exposures from wild fish broth among Inuit pregnant women</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/groleau2025-inuit-fish-broth-metals-pregnancy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-cooking-hijiki-make-it-lower-in-arsenic" data-anchor="does-cooking-hijiki-make-it-lower-in-arsenic" data-question="Does cooking hijiki make it lower in arsenic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does cooking hijiki make it lower in arsenic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Yes, if the soaking and cooking water is discarded.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Laparra JM, Velez D, Montoro R, Barbera R, Farre R · 2003</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Estimation of Arsenic Bioaccessibility in Edible Seaweed by an in Vitro Digestion Method</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Soaking and boiling together removed most arsenic in Japanese tests, and boiling alone lowered inorganic arsenic from 54 to 31 mg/kg dry weight.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Laparra JM, Velez D, Montoro R, Barbera R, Farre R · 2003</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Estimation of Arsenic Bioaccessibility in Edible Seaweed by an in Vitro Digestion Method</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/laparra2003-seaweed-arsenic-bioaccessibility">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Prepared hijiki in the UK still averaged 11 mg/kg inorganic arsenic wet weight, far above other prepared seaweeds.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Heavy metal mitigation and remediation for seaweed

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Controls for seaweed act at four points: species and type choice, growing site and harvest, processing, and household preparation. The best supported are choosing low-arsenic types and kelp species, which changes inorganic arsenic by two orders of magnitude, and soaking then boiling with the water discarded, which removes much of the arsenic that remains.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Arsenic in seaweed—Forms, concentration and dietary exposure</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Chemical Toxicology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rose2007-seaweed-arsenic-forms-uk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ichikawa S, Kamoshida M, Hanaoka K, Hamano M, Maitani T, Kaise T · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Decrease of arsenic in edible brown algae Hijikia fusiforme by the cooking process</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Organometallic Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ichikawa2006-hijiki-cooking-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ownsworth E, Selby D, Ottley CJ, Unsworth E, Raab A, Feldmann J, Sproson AD, Kuroda J, Faidutti C, Bucker P · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Tracing the natural and anthropogenic influence on the trace elemental chemistry of estuarine macroalgae and the implications for human consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ownsworth2019-estuarine-macroalgae-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Siting and harvest controls are observational: farmed sugar kelp in northern Norway had more than four times the cadmium of southern farms, and using the old blade tip rather than the base lowered cadmium in New England kelp.<sup class="cite">[[sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Duinker A, Kleppe M, Fjare E, Biancarosa I, Heldal HE, Dahl L, Lunestad BT · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Knowledge update on macroalgae food and feed safety</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Rapport fra Havforskningen</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/duinker2020-macroalgae-food-feed-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/shaughnessy2023-sugar-kelp-new-england-metals|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaughnessy B K, Jackson B P, Byrnes J E K · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" →</a></span></span></sup>

Linked analytes, repeated seasons and reports are not independent studies.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Effects and comparators</p><div class="hmi-selected-result"><p><strong>Inorganic arsenic</strong><span class="hmi-direction-badge hmi-comparison-lower"><svg class="hmi-direction-icon" viewBox="0 0 21 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M2 22V6h4v16zm6 0V12h4v10zm6 0v-4h4v4z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></svg><span><strong class="hmi-direction-label">Decreased</strong><span class="hmi-comparison-value">Lower inorganic arsenic in the solid seaweed</span></span></span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Inorganic arsenic loss</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail">Soup preparation (75–96% loss)</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note">Dry weight</span><span class="hmi-comparison-detail hmi-row-note"><strong>Not quantified</strong> · No supported numerical treatment contrast is retained for this finding. A direction, market association, source-selection strategy or guidance statement alone does not establish a percentage change.</span></p></div><p>Same seaweed before and after each preparation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">How magnitude is classified</p><p>HMI editorial magnitude bands: Low is a change greater than 0% and below 25%; Moderate is 25% to below 50%; High is 50% or more, relative to that control’s own comparator. Direction is shown separately. These are descriptive display bands, not validated efficacy cutoffs, occurrence-baseline positions, statistical significance, evidence certainty, safety or net benefit. A range spanning bands retains both labels; a qualitative label has no implied percentage.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Control in context</p><p>A soup preparation removed 75–96% of inorganic arsenic from the solid seaweed, a cold soak about 65% and a 10–20 second blanch 3–61%; the arsenic moved into the liquid.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Context</th><th scope="col">Selected control</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Material</td><td>Scottish and Japanese kelp</td></tr><tr><td>Stage</td><td>home preparation</td></tr><tr><td>Audience</td><td>Ingredient suppliers · Brands · Consumers</td></tr><tr><td>Period</td><td>As reported</td></tr><tr><td>Conditions</td><td>Kelp eaten after soaking or cooking; the soup liquid keeps the arsenic.</td></tr><tr><td>Tested scale</td><td>Laboratory</td></tr><tr><td>Sample units</td><td>Source sampling units; no independent intervention units unless stated.</td></tr><tr><td>Trade-offs</td><td>Iodine, texture and other metals change with the same step; not quantified unless stated.</td></tr><tr><td>Verification</td><td>Confirm with lot results that report inorganic arsenic by speciation and state the basis.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Design, applicability and operating conditions</p><p>Measured preparation or processing comparison. class="cite-card-journal">Analytica Chimica Acta</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/garcia-salgado2012-edible-algae-arsenic-speciation">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup that product.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rose M, Lewis J, Langford N, Baxter M, Origgi S, Barber M, MacBain H, Thomas K · 2007</span><a class="cite-card-title" EFSA estimated that adult high consumers of hijiki eating 10 g a day of prepared hijiki would take in about 1.6 µg/kg body weight per day of inorganic arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|36]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A Spanish survey calculated that 1.7 g a day of one dried hijiki product would reach the former WHO tolerable weekly intake for inorganic arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/almela2002-algae-food-arsenic-metals|37]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Almela C, Algora S, Benito V, Clemente MJ, Devesa V, Súñer MA, Vélez D, Montoro R · 2002</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/almela2002-algae-food-arsenic-metals">Heavy Metal, Total Arsenic, and Inorganic Arsenic Contents of Algae Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/almela2002-algae-food-arsenic-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>
